extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and activists interested in feminism, gender studies, sexual harassment, and online/social media abuse
extracted.subtask_description: Describing, defining, and characterizing 'slut-shaming' as a social phenomenon: what counts as it, who practices it, contexts where it appears, its consequences, and responses/activism. Useful for diagnosing incidents, analyzing discourse, or developing interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core definition of slut-shaming
rubrics_metrics.description: "Slut-shaming is the practice of criticizing individuals, particularly but not exclusively women and girls, who violate expectations of behavior and appearance regarding issues related to sexuality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term covers criticism for behaviors, appearance, or desires considered too sexual by societal norms. It may also apply to gay men who face disapproval for promiscuous sexual behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete examples of slut-shaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include criticism or punishment for: violating dress code policies by dressing in sexually provocative ways; requesting access to birth control; having premarital, extramarital, casual, or promiscuous sex; or engaging in prostitution or other sex work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also includes victim-blaming for being raped or otherwise sexually assaulted. Use these concrete acts as indicators when classifying behavior as slut-shaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic mechanism — transgression of sexual codes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Slut-shaming involves criticizing women for their transgression of accepted codes of sexual conduct, i.e., admonishing them for behavior, attire or desires that are more sexual than society finds acceptable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the normative boundary being policed: the criticism targets perceived excess sexualness relative to local norms rather than objective harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetrators and double standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Slut-shaming may be practiced by men and women. One study found women slut-shamed more than men, and women who slut-shame other women continuously apply unfavorable sexual double standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both gender of perpetrator and whether double standards (different judgments for men vs women) are being applied when evaluating incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim blaming in sexual assault contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: The term is also used to describe victim blaming for rape and other sexual assault by stating the crime was caused (either in part or in full) by the woman wearing revealing clothing or acting in a sexually provocative manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify rhetorical moves that shift responsibility from perpetrator to victim (e.g., 'she was asking for it') as core signs of slut-shaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social function — punishment, sexism, and intrasexual competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Slut-shaming can be a form of social punishment, sexism, and female intrasexual competition for social status. The term 'slut' reduces the value of a woman and violates gender roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing social dynamics, look for uses of shaming to regulate status, enforce gender norms, or exclude individuals from social groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychosocial and public-health consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexually permissive individuals can be at risk of social isolation; slut-shaming functions as social bullying and can have tangible negative public health consequences (e.g., discouraging men who have sex with men from accessing HIV prevention like PrEP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider measurable outcomes such as social isolation, mental health effects, reduced healthcare access, and increased vulnerability to violence or suicide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online/social media manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: Slut-shaming is prevalent on social media platforms (YouTube, Instagram, Twitter, Facebook), occurring as insults, harassment, revenge pornography, rape and death threats, and other forms of online sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include abusive language, distributed intimate images without consent, coordinated harassment campaigns, and platform-specific tagging/hashtags used to shame targets. Note prevalence data: e.g., Pew found high rates of young women being called offensive names online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical pattern — 'asked for it' implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Slut-shaming implies that victims of sex violence 'asked for it' because they were sexually promiscuous or dressed provocatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot arguments that attribute causation of assault to victims' attire/behavior as a particular class of slut-shaming with legal and moral implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reappropriation and activism (resignification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Activism (e.g., SlutWalk) has embraced the slut-shame label and engaged in resignification: reclaiming 'slut' as a source of power and shifting focus back to perpetrators rather than victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating responses, note tactics of reclaiming language, public demonstrations, and cultural productions (plays, podcasts) intended to destigmatize sexuality and reduce shaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersectional amplification — race and class (Black women)
rubrics_metrics.description: Black women are disproportionately affected by slut-shaming due to misogynoir and historical myths (e.g., the 'Jezebel' stereotype); low-income women are also at greater risk, and high-status women can use resources to mitigate shaming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply an intersectional lens: assess how race, class, and historical stereotypes amplify shaming and limit recourse; look for media/industry representations (e.g., hip hop) that hypersexualize Black women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual orientation and gender nuances — gay/bisexual men
rubrics_metrics.description: Gay and bisexual men are also victimized through slut-shaming; it can discourage discussing sexual practices with healthcare providers and hinder prevention measures (e.g., PrEP uptake).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that slut-shaming is not only gendered against women: consider how it operates among men and affects public health and social support networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual orientation and gender nuances — lesbian and bisexual women
rubrics_metrics.description: Lesbian and bisexual women face slut-shaming and fetishization (e.g., being reduced to a 'porn category'); bisexual women are often bullied by other women for perceived sexual 'openness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between shaming based on sexual behavior and shaming based on identity/fetishization. Note how porn industry representations contribute to shaming and objectification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical indicators from social research
rubrics_metrics.description: Research findings used to identify slut-shaming include vignette studies (e.g., Cornell study where women rated a peer with many partners as less competent, emotionally stable, warm, and dominant) and surveys showing differential harassment rates by age and gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey/vignette outcomes, prevalence statistics, and qualitative accounts as evidentiary criteria when documenting or studying slut-shaming in a population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and cultural context as analytic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no single origin date for the term; its discussion grew from longer histories of sexual policing, with notable prominence during the late 2000s and connections to second-wave feminism and sexual revolutions of the 1960s–70s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate incidents in cultural and historical context—trends in sexual norms, media coverage, and feminist movements inform how shaming is produced and contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of resistance and remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses include legal action against online harassment, community-led campaigns (e.g., petitions to train law enforcement on online sexual violence), and cultural works (plays, podcasts) that raise awareness and support victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposed remedies by whether they shift blame to perpetrators, provide resources to victims, change institutional responses, or alter public discourse (reduction of shaming language).
